doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Concerto for Cootie and context in music
summary: The ending of Concerto for Cootie shows a major seventh on a dominant chord; context is where you are, where from, where to.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. So there’s a great example. So the thing that I found with Clare and Duke is that a lot of times when I would find I’d hear this voice and go oh, what is that? Sometimes it would be something that I wouldn’t think of playing, and sometimes I’d realize oh it’s just the same voicing but the notes are rearranged so it gets a different color. We were talking about improvising and using a major seventh on a dominant chord, it’s the same thing with writing. Like at the end of “Concerto for Cootie,” after you hear the statement of the theme [plays piano], again he ends up on a D flat chord and it’s in the key of F, so

he’s on the flat sixth [plays piano]. And the clarinet’s up here but with the alto. Cootie Williams plays the five-one, and the first thing you hear against this tonic note is G flat 7 [plays piano]. So that’s not only a way of making a major seventh on a dominant seventh sound great, but it makes that F 6 chord that comes afterwards sound great too. Because it’s not the chords that you use, it’s how you get there and where you go from there. So one of the things I also try to impart to the students as much as possible, whether it’s improvising or composing and arranging, that context is everything. And context, the simplest way I understand context is where I’m at, how did I get here, and where is this going? The place that you are, the thing immediately before that, and then what’s going to follow it.
